text: iCall India: 9152987821. Run by TISS (Tata Institute of Social Sciences), Mumbai. Available Monday to Saturday, 8am to 10pm. Free, confidential, and run by trained counselors — not volunteers. Offers support in Hindi and English. Also offers email counseling at icall@tiss.edu. iCall is one of the most professionally staffed helplines in India and has specific support for LGBTQ+ callers.

Vandrevala Foundation Helpline: 1860-2662-345. Available 24 hours, 7 days a week. Free of cost. Supports Hindi, English, and multiple regional languages. Staffed by trained mental health professionals. Also accessible via WhatsApp. One of the few helplines genuinely available in the middle of the night — critical for acute crisis situations.

AASRA: 9820466627. Mumbai-based but serves nationally. Available 24/7. Focused specifically on suicide prevention and emotional support. AASRA volunteers are trained in active listening and de-escalation. Also reachable at 022-27546669. For callers in suicidal crisis who need a patient, non-judgmental listener, AASRA is a reliable first call.

Snehi: 044-24640050. Chennai-based NGO providing emotional support helpline. Serves nationally. Trained volunteer listeners available for distress calls. Also runs support for people dealing with grief, loneliness, and relationship issues — not just acute suicidal crisis. An important resource in South India.

NIMHANS Helpline: 080-46110007. Run by the National Institute of Mental Health and Neuro Sciences in Bengaluru. Provides mental health triage and referral. NIMHANS also has a walk-in outpatient department. For Bengaluru residents in crisis, NIMHANS emergency unit is available for psychiatric emergencies with no prior appointment needed.

Sahai Bangalore: 080-25497777. Bengaluru-based crisis helpline. Available evenings and weekends. Provides emotional support in Kannada, Hindi, and English. Primarily serves the Bengaluru population but can provide national referrals. Run by trained counselors with a focus on accessible, stigma-free support.

Connecting NGO Pune: 9922001122. Pune-based helpline providing suicide prevention and emotional support services. Available in Marathi, Hindi, and English. Run by trained volunteers and counselors. A key resource for people in Maharashtra outside Mumbai who need localized support.

iCall Maharashtra — additional access: Beyond the national number (9152987821), iCall operates email counseling (icall@tiss.edu) and has conducted outreach in colleges across Maharashtra. Students in TISS partner institutions can access on-campus counseling referrals through iCall. Walk-in appointments are available at TISS Mumbai campus.

Tele-MANAS — 14416: National Tele Mental Health Programme launched by Government of India. Call 14416 or 1-800-891-4416 (toll free). Available 24/7. Services in 20+ languages. Connects callers to trained counselors and, if needed, to psychiatrists and district mental health programs. Launched 2022, expanding coverage across all states and union territories.

What to say when calling a helpline: You don't need a script. Start simply: 'Main bahut mushkil waqt se guzar raha hoon aur baat karna chahta tha.' You don't need to have a diagnosis or explain everything. Helpline counselors are trained to ask gentle questions. You can say: 'I don't know where to start.' That is enough. You can remain anonymous. You don't have to give your name.

What to expect on a helpline call: The counselor will introduce themselves, ask why you're calling, and listen without judgment. They won't call the police unless you're in immediate danger and give specific location. They won't tell your family without your consent. They may suggest resources or follow-up. Calls can be as short as 5 minutes or as long as an hour. There is no 'wrong' reason to call.

Safety planning — Step 1, Warning Signs: Identify personal warning signs that a crisis is building — specific thoughts ('I'm worthless'), feelings (intense hopelessness), behaviors (isolating, giving things away), or situations (fights with family, failing exams). Writing these down makes it easier to recognize the spiral before it peaks.

Safety planning — Step 2, Internal Coping Strategies: List things you can do alone to manage distress: walk, listen to music, do breathing exercises, write in journal, watch a show. These are first-line coping before reaching out. Having a written list matters because in crisis, memory and problem-solving shut down.

Safety planning — Step 3, Social Contacts for Distraction: List 2-3 people or places that provide distraction — not necessarily crisis support. 'Call Rohan just to chat.' 'Go to chai tapri nearby.' The goal here is distraction and connection, not necessarily disclosing the crisis.

Safety planning — Step 4, People to Ask for Help: List 2-3 trusted people who know about your struggles and can be called in crisis. Include their phone numbers. 'Agar main khud se nahi sambhal pa raha, main [naam] ko call karunga.' These are people who won't panic, won't judge, and will stay with you.

Safety planning — Step 5, Professionals and Crisis Lines: Write down your therapist's contact, nearest psychiatric emergency, and 2-3 helpline numbers. Include: iCall 9152987821, Vandrevala 1860-2662-345, Tele-MANAS 14416. This step ensures help is accessible at 2am when you can't think clearly.

Safety planning — Step 6, Making the Environment Safe: Remove or restrict access to means of self-harm during a high-risk period. Give medications to a family member. Lock away sharp objects. Temporarily move out if the home environment is a trigger. Means restriction is one of the most evidence-supported suicide prevention interventions.

Safety planning — Step 7, Reasons for Living: Write down personal reasons for living — specific people, future goals, pets, unfinished dreams. 'Meri chhoti behen ko meri zaroorat hai.' 'Main Ladakh trip karna chahta tha.' During peak crisis, reading this list creates a pause. The plan ends with a signature — a commitment to follow the steps before acting.

ALGEE crisis first aid model: A — Approach the person, assess safety, and introduce yourself. L — Listen non-judgmentally using open body language and reflective responses. G — Give support and information, don't minimize. E — Encourage professional help — offer to help them call. E — Encourage other support (self-help strategies, trusted people). ALGEE is used internationally for mental health first aid training.

Warning signs of suicidal intent in others: Giving away prized possessions without explanation. Saying goodbyes as if they won't see you again. Sudden calm after a long period of depression — this can signal a decision has been made. Researching methods online. Withdrawing from everyone. Statements like 'everyone would be better off without me.' Any combination warrants a direct, caring conversation.

How to ask directly about suicide: Suicidality ke baare mein seedha poochna safe hai — it does not plant the idea. Say: 'Main tumse seedha poochna chahta hoon — kya tumhare mann mein khud ko hurt karne ya zindagi khatam karne ke khayal aa rahe hain?' Asking directly shows you're not scared of the answer and opens the door for honest conversation.

Means restriction — evidence base: Research consistently shows that restricting access to lethal means reduces suicide deaths — not just shifts the method. When families remove firearms, stockpiled medications, or other means during a high-risk period, suicide risk decreases measurably. Gently discuss means restriction with the person's trusted family member or caregiver — framed as a temporary, caring precaution.

Passive vs active suicidal ideation — both need attention: 'Mujhe zindagi mein koi interest nahi' or 'kaash main soja aur uthne ki zaroorat na ho' is passive ideation — no active intent, but still clinically significant. Active ideation with plan and intent is a psychiatric emergency. Both require follow-up, safety assessment, and support — neither should be normalized or dismissed.

De-escalation language in crisis: Validate without agreeing: 'Yeh sach mein bahut mushkil hai — main samajh sakta hoon kyun tune aisa feel kiya.' Avoid: 'You have so much to live for' (invalidating), 'don't be dramatic' (shaming), 'think of your family' (guilt-inducing). These phrases make people less likely to disclose. Stay curious: 'Mujhe aur batao — yeh kab se chal raha hai?'

After a crisis — follow-up protocol: The 24-48 hours after a crisis peak are high-risk for a second episode. Key steps: don't leave the person alone in the immediate aftermath. Check in by message or call the next day. Help them schedule the next appointment with their therapist or psychiatrist. Review the safety plan. Remove means if not already done. Normalize that recovery isn't linear.

Crisis for teens — school counselor as first contact: Agar koi teen crisis mein hai, school counselor first institutional contact hona chahiye. In India, CBSE mandates school counselors but availability varies widely. Teens may be more comfortable disclosing to a peer or older student first — peer support programs (like YourDOST campus) train students to identify and refer distressed classmates.

Parents' role in teen crisis: Parents often feel guilty, scared, or defensive when their child discloses suicidal thoughts. Key guidance: listen without interrogating, don't immediately problem-solve, don't minimize ('board exams mein sab stress mein hote hain'), don't threaten punishment. Take all disclosures seriously. Involve a mental health professional within 24 hours. Stay connected and calm.

Crisis for domestic violence survivors: Domestic violence crisis differs from suicidal crisis — the risk is from an external person. Key resources: Women's Helpline 181 (national), iCall 9152987821, police emergency 100. One Stop Centres (Sakhi Centres) under government mandate provide integrated support — shelter, medical, legal, and psychological help under one roof across most districts.

De-escalation for chatbot conversations: Agar user crisis mein hai chatbot pe: immediately validate ('yeh sun ke dukh hua, main yahaan hoon'), don't continue assessment or psychoeducation, give 2-3 specific helpline numbers, ask if they are safe right now, ask if there is someone who can be with them. Offer to stay in conversation if they're not ready to call. Do not abruptly end conversation.

Psychiatric emergency — when to call 112: If a person is in immediate danger of harming themselves or others, is unconscious, or has already attempted self-harm, call 112 (national emergency). In this situation, confidentiality gives way to duty of care. In India, NIMHANS and government hospital psychiatric emergency units are equipped to handle acute psychiatric crises. Inform the emergency team it is a mental health situation.
